#1370. George & Armstrong Start In England Under-21s Friendly

Harrison Armstrong and Tyrique George both played an hour of England Under-21s’ 1-0 defeat to Portugal at Ashton Gate Stadium.

The Young Lions went behind to an Afonso Moreira goal in the 28th minute and were unable to find a way past keeper João Carvalho from there.

This was Armstrong’s first start for the Under-21s after making his debut as a substitute against Ireland in the previous international window, while George was making his 10th appearance at this level.

Lee Carsley’s side had already secured qualification for next summer’s UEFA U21 Euro finals in October, and are using these friendlies in preparation for the tournament in Albania and Serbia.

Armstrong and George return to action in Bristol on Monday 16 November, taking on France (7.30pm kick-off).

#1369. Carlo Ancelotti and Raphinha see red: Security separate furious Brazil stars from officials after shock 3-2 defeat by Japan - with manager and captain sent off in bad-tempered friendly

Published: 11:31 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 12:52 EST, 14 November 2026

Carlo Ancelotti hit out at an 'inexperienced' referee after the Brazil boss and captain Raphinha were sent off in the closing stages of their shock 3-2 defeat by Japan.

Security staff were required to enter the pitch at full time to separate players from the officials, with Brazil having been left furious over the nature of Japan's stoppage time winner.

Ancelotti and Raphinha, who had been substituted, were among those to furiously protest following Tatsuhiro Sakamoto's late strike.

Singaporean referee Jansen Foo Chuan Hui had allowed play to continue after Takumi Minamino had made multiple challenges on Brazil midfielder Joao Gomes, before eventually coming away with the ball.

Amid Brazilian appeals for a foul, Japan launched a late attack with Sakamoto ultimately lifting the ball over goalkeeper Pedro Morisco.

Brazilian protests continued despite Japan's winner being confirmed by VAR, with Ancelotti and Raphinha being shown red cards by the referee for their reactions.

Security staff intervened after Brazil stars confronted the referee after their 3-2 defeat by Japan

Carlo Ancelotti was sent off as Brazil were beaten in stoppage time in their friendly in Singapore

Ancelotti criticised the 'inexperienced' referee following the match and revealed he had been told he had been sent off for failing to control his bench

🚨🚨| Raphinha and Carlo Ancelotti have been SENT OFF for Protesting. 🟥😳 pic.twitter.com/YoXrZW9N0U

'He gave me the red card because he said I was not able to control the bench, and that all the players were on the field, that is the reason,' Ancelotti said.

Ancelotti added: 'A pity the result, because we don't like to lose the game, but we have to look at what we did well. There are many things. Some players who played for the first time, who showed good quality. For 70 minutes, the team was good.

'The result, obviously, is conditioned by the attitude of the referee, who did not blow the whistle.

'But it's not his fault; it was a high-level match, and I think he didn't have the experience to manage this type of match.'

Barcelona star Raphinha claimed post-match that Brazil had also been angered over a potential handball in the build-up to Japan's opening goal, as well as seeing a penalty appeal waved away.

'First of all, I'd like to take this opportunity to apologise for my behaviour and for being sent off,' Raphinha told Globo.

'Sometimes it's hard to keep calm, especially after what I felt were so many refereeing errors during the match. I tried to speak to him several times, and not once did I feel he was open to discussion. I believe that he made many errors throughout the game, and that is unacceptable.

'In my view, their first goal involved a foul where the opponent took the ball off me with his hand. I think it's a foul, but I can understand why it wasn't given based on the current law.

Brazil captain Raphinha was also dismissed amid their protests over Japan's winning goal

Brazil had been convinced there had been a foul in the build-up to Tatsuhiro Sakamoto's winner

'Then there was the penalty in the first half, in my opinion it was a penalty, but he said no. Then, for their third goal, there was a clear foul on Joao Gomes. With the help of VAR, he eventually allowed the goal. It's very difficult not to talk about the refereeing.'

Brazil had fallen 2-0 down in the friendly with Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura scoring in the opening 20 minutes at Singapore's National Stadium.

Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr scored twice to level the match before Sakamoto's controversial late winner.

It is the second time Japan have beaten Brazil 3-2 in the past 18 months, but the five-time world champions did win 2-1 in their last-32 meeting at this summer's World Cup.

#1368. Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

If the verdicts are upheld, of course, it wasn’t their penthouse and it wasn’t their caviar.

When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside.

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won’t forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let’s get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.

PSG have made a slow start to their Ligue 1 campaign, their worst since Luis Enrique’s first season in charge. Starting with two draws and a defeat, they have rallied with three successive victories to climb up to sixth as the head coach, as he tends to do in the league, rotates his midfielders and forwards like crazy, to whose ranks he has added the World Cup-winner Ferran Torres. The summer signing scored a hat-trick in his Champions League debut for the club, a 6-1 mauling of Slovan Bratislava.

City, too, started their European campaign with a win, Erling Haaland scoring both goals in the 2-0 victory over Porto at the Dragao and you won’t need me to remind you that they have won all six of their Premier League games to lead Arsenal by three points at the top of the table.

#1366. My Story: O’Brien's Diabetes Diagnosis & Journey Into Football

To mark World Diabetes Day, we revisiting a chat with Everton defender Jake O’Brien, who sat down to discuss his experiences with the condition.

A Republic of Ireland international, O'Brien also covered a wide range of topics including his journey into professional football and an impressive sporting background.

O’Brien was diagnosed with type one diabetes aged 16 – and recalling that time, he explained: “There were a few weeks when I was ill. I was losing a lot of weight and was very tired. I was drinking eight or nine litres of water a day.

“I realised something wasn’t right. I went to the doctor’s and they sent me up to hospital and diagnosed me with it. My pancreas, basically, doesn’t work; it doesn’t produce insulin.

"It’s a genetic thing, I suppose, but in that sense, no one in my family has ever had it."

#1365. So much pace and potential, not enough positive impact... surely Scotland must now redefine the role of Ben Gannon-Doak?

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 12:41 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 13:14 EST, 14 November 2026

In an age where much of the football on show in the English Premier League is so robotic as to be almost unwatchable, flashes of individual brilliance are increasingly becoming things to be cherished.

Across his time at Liverpool and Bournemouth, Ben Gannon-Doak has sporadically distinguished himself as someone who can light up a game by doing something out of the blue and out of the ordinary.

As many a defender will testify, that electric burst of pace across a short distance makes him unplayable at times. He has an X-factor which sets him apart from the crowd.

What a shame that injuries have restricted his number of appearances to this point. Since moving south from Celtic in 2022, including a loan spell with Middlesbrough, Gannon-Doak has played fewer than 50 times.

At the very time in his career when he could have done with smoothing off the rough edges, he’s spent far too long rehabilitating from one setback or another.

In the build-up to Friday’s match with North Macedonia, Sebastien Pocognoli spoke about how encouraged he was that the player was finally seeing more game time on the south coast, partly as a result of the team’s maiden voyage in Europe.

Ben Gannon-Doak started in a right wing-back role and had an energetic yet frustrating night

The hope of all concerned was that the recent run of matches which the winger had so evidently needed would translate into a more accomplished display in a Scotland jersey. Alas, this proved to be wishful thinking.

Even against very ordinary opposition, Gannon-Doak’s display proved to be another frustrating watch for the Tartan Army.

Time and time again, he brought them to the edge of their seats by facing up a white jersey and seemingly disappearing in a puff of smoke towards the line. Rarely, however, did the end product materialise.

For a winger with such blinding speed to continually struggle with the all-important final ball is a difficult thing to repeatedly witness.

We shall never know, of course, if the player’s crossing ability would be better by this stage if he hadn’t endured such wretched luck with injuries. But you suspect it’s now just about as good as it’s ever going to be.

The trouble for Pocognoli is that the quality of the delivery from wing-backs into the penalty box is arguably the most important facet of his preferred 3-4-3 system.

When it breaks down, as it did so often against the group outsiders, the whole thing threatens to grind to a halt.

Gannon-Doak's crossing remains an area of concern for Scotland given his wide position

On his record-equalling 102nd cap, Andy Robertson was also guilty of being wasteful on the other flank. Given we know what the skipper has delivered down the years, though, we can write that off as merely a bad night at the office.

The difference with Gannon-Doak is that we’ve rarely seen him tear it up on the flank in a Scotland jersey. So much pace and potential. Not enough positive outcomes when it comes to delivering crosses. In 21 matches, he has three assists and one goal. Those aren’t great numbers.

Just how long do you persevere with a player who doesn’t look to have the requisite skill set for such a specialised and vital position?

Aaron Hickey clearly doesn’t have the pace of the man who he replaced late on, yet he’s hardly a slouch. He is, though, more switched on defensively. And he does know how to cross a football.

It was telling that Gannon-Doak’s most positive contribution of the night against the group outsiders came when he left his station to move infield and take Oli McBurnie’s pass in his stride with the score standing at one-apiece.

His surge towards the goal initially looked like it had been hampered by a heavy touch only for VAR to correctly identify that he’d been impeded by the goalkeeper. He earned his corn in that moment.

John McGinn’s conversion from 12 yards, his second goal of the night, spared Pocognoli’s blushes after a display which didn’t exactly inspire.

That sequence of play certainly raised the possibility that Gannon-Doak could be utilised to better effect in another role.

Gannon-Doak's forward burst led to the award of a penalty and hinted at an alternative role

If played more centrally, his crossing – undoubtedly his weak spot – would not be such an issue. But the acceleration and driving runs would still be there to cause chaos in and around the penalty box. That will always be his strong suit.

To get the best out of him, maybe the manager needs to redefine him.

Any redeployment would, obviously, create another issue. If Pocognoli remains wedded to the current system, it seems likely that Billy Gilmour and Lewis Ferguson will occupy the two holding berths.

Ahead of them, and behind the main striker, McGinn and Scott McTominay are virtually undroppable. It might be the case then, that Gannon-Doak is eventually utilised as an impact sub. Yet, it would not be a plan without its merits.

He’s got a part to play in this set-up. Probably just not where he’s currently being positioned.

You’d be surprised, frankly, if he started in St Gallen on Monday. Switzerland are a far superior side to North Macedonia, already assured of promotion to League A by topping the section and looking to end this campaign with a flourish against a Scotland side they beat comfortably at Hampden.

They’ll ask far more questions of Pocognoli’s side. It feels like a task more suited to Hickey.

Scotland, collectively, will need to buck up their ideas if they are to stand any chance of emerging with a positive outcome or, at the least, some credit.

Scotland fans are desperate to see Gannon-Doak succeed but a little change might be needed

There was a flatness to Friday’s performance, especially in a first half in which the much-vaunted high-press was conspicuous by its absence.

The passing was too safe and predictable. The tempo was low and the play was unimaginative. By half-time, the visitors had fashioned the better chance when Enis Bardhi smashed the ball into the side net.

Scotland were markedly better after the turnaround. After Billy Gilmour’s scarcely believable miss, they were deserving of the opener which came when McGinn burst into the box and lashed home after fine work from Che Adams.

Stemming straight from a corner, North Macedonia’s equaliser – which ended their eight-game goal drought – asked a serious question of Pocognoli’s players.

To their credit, they stepped up with Gannon-Doak’s foray into the box causing the moment of indecision on which the game swung.

The manner of a first Hampden win for Pocognoli won’t live long in the memory. The fervent hope is that it proves to be the start of something.

#1364. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

#1363. Toffees Make It Five Unbeaten With Spurs Stalemate

Everton made it five games unbeaten with a hard-fought goalless draw away at high-flying Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday afternoon.

The result sees the Blues continue their strong form having thrashed Durham 6-0 on Wednesday following two stalemates against Chelsea and Manchester United in the WSL.

Ruby Mace grabbed the Player of the Match award in the capital – the midfielder repeating her award-winning performance at the home of the North Londoners last term.

It was the visitors who created the first real opportunity inside 17 minutes as Ornella Vignola teed the in-form Yuka Momiki on the edge of the area. The forward, who netted a hat-trick in the 6-0 win in midweek, looked to curl past Lize Kop, but saw her placed effort saved by the diving keeper.

History repeated itself only ten minutes later as Momiki saw another strike palmed away by the keeper. The 30-year-old drifted inside from the right and let fly upon reaching the edge of the box. Unfortunately, Kop anticipated the shot and collected after initially spilling the ball.

The hosts responded on 39 minutes as Courtney Brosnan was called in to action to deny Julie Blakstad. After breaching the Blues’ box, the Norwegian feinted before unleashing a rising strike at goal. Brosnan leapt up to tip the ball over the upright, though.

That concluded the action for a tight, physical opening 45; with Blakstad coming close once more five minutes after the interval.

Found at the back-post, the winger fired at goal and seemed destined to get on the scoresheet. However, Hannah Blundell burst forward to narrow the angle and bravely block, evading the danger.

At the other end, Everton caught Spurs on the break after Momiki held the ball up well on the halfway line. Clare Wheeler threaded it through to the advancing Vignola, who raced at goal with the ball at her feet. She pulled the trigger when faced one-on-one with Kop, but saw her low-strike sail agonisingly wide of the far-post.

Brosnan produced another fine stop five minutes later, the keeper denying Cathinka Tandenberg on this occasion. The Norway-international got down low in an attempt to nestle the ball in to the bottom right corner. Somehow, Brosnan reacted rapidly to palm it away for a corner.

Moments later, Blakstad threatened again – the forward rattling the upright on this occasion. She cut-in past Rosa van Gool and let fly, the ball striking the frame of the goal on its way out.

Head coach Scott Phelan made his first change of the game with 12 minutes remaining as Noemie Mouchon, who scored a brace against Durham on Wednesday, replaced Momiki.

The striker almost had an instant impact as she forced Kop in to a smart save. Rion Ishikawa did brilliantly down the unfamiliar right to dance past two challenges before chipping it through to the substitute. Mouchon came inside before unleashing a curling effort that was caught well by the retreating Kop.

The France-youth international came even closer in the dying minutes as she had a chance similar to Vignola previously. Like her teammate, Mouchon’s strike whistled just wide of the far-post from the right-hand side of the box.

The referee then concluded the affair, with attention now turning to Everton’s Players Cup tie with Manchester United on Wednesday night (7pm KO).

#1361. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

Rogers’s reprieve changed all that. Inexplicably inconsistent as Tierney was, Chelsea exhibited a steel which thrilled Alonso as much as those games when Cole Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro are in full flow.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

He told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

“The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”

However, given the good start to the season for Everton so far, he does not have too much rancour.

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Xabi Alonso gives relatively positive news on Emi Martinez.

He describes the planned tests as “precautionary” and says, “as far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.”

Neto added more detail to his thoughts on the game.

On his first goal, he explained how Everton’s defensive approach allowed them to react: “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”

He credited his Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, with his calmness in front of goal, adding: “This comes a little bit from the new coach of the national team that says when you are near to the area you need to pass to the goal, so really happy with that.”

With Chelsea now in the Champions League places, Neto was keen to keep up the momentum. He said: “It’s really important. We know it’s tough to play away, even at home there are no easy games. We came here with personality, with good intentions to win the match and really happy with the result.”

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1360. Mauricio Pochettino leaves behind a negligible legacy at USMNT... where raised standards never materialized into results as tearful Argentine bolts for Man United

Published: 13:29 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 13:42 EST, 14 November 2026

Perhaps it's incredibly cynical, and maybe too harsh, to call the tears that fell down the face of Mauricio Pochettino 'performative.' But it's the first word that came to mind – followed by 'surprising' and 'a bit much.'

It was only four months ago when the Argentine who had been atop the United States' men's national team since 2024 signed a contract extension to stay on board for another four years.

'We want to try to have a lasting impact on the sport in the country that has welcomed us so warmly and for that impact to extend beyond results on the field,' Pochettino said when his contract was signed.

Yet, after a few months and one international window, that experiment to make a 'lasting impact' has ended. Pochettino may have cried because he fell in love with the country, but it's not like he got fired. Instead, he's off to lead one of the world's greatest football brands in Manchester United.

So now the question turns to the legacy Pochettino leaves behind. Plenty of American soccer writers and fans point to the spirit the former Chelsea boss created and how he helped to energize a team which had been bogged down by past coaches.

But Pochettino's results don't scream success. The World Cup finish was nothing special compared to his peers, his record against the best nations the USA faced was poor and he'll leave as the first full-time USMNT manager in nearly 30 years to not win at least one trophy.

Mauricio Pochettino cried as he left the United States' top job for Manchester United

Pochettino's USMNT played exciting football, but ultimately didn't progress past the norm

But any potential for further growth evaporated when the Argentine returned to England

By all accounts, the greatest thing Pochettino did was install a hungry, all-in-or-nothing culture in a team bogged down by an earth-rocking scandal and a poor 2024 Copa America run.

But he did so in a way that often left the biggest players of the USMNT system behind. Rather than keep a consistent core of his best players around, he seemed intent on tinkering with the lineup in each window.

The results reflect that instability. Leading to the World Cup, Pochettino played 12 games against sides in the top 30 of the FIFA World Rankings. He won just three fixtures – drawing once and losing the remaining eight.

All the while, he was linked to returns to Europe. Pochettino may have said in his exit press conference that he 'never said I wanted to go back to the Premier League' but the Premier League certainly wanted him – especially Tottenham.

Come World Cup time, Pochettino's team finally seemed to gel with a scintillating style of play never before seen in the USMNT.

But it all crashed down after the Round of 32 game against Bosnia when Folarin Balogun's red card was (as this American will admit) deviously overturned. The noise and controversy led to the Americans' embarrassment at the hands of Belgium on home soil.

A summer of exciting soccer for the USMNT followed years of hard resets and mixed results

It all fell apart with a demolition by Belgium, leaving Pochettino without any success

The Yanks were not expected to go much further than the last 16. But branding Pochettino's time atop the USMNT a 'success' on the back of this World Cup performance is giving him too much credit – especially considering the four prior managers to take the US to the World Cup all made it to that stage of the tournament as well.

With his departure confirmed, Pochettino is the first USMNT manager to leave the post without any silverware since the 1998 departure of Steve Sampson, who hadn't been a professional manager before being appointed to the job.

Even though he achieved little in terms of results, players praised Pochettino's leadership and development skills, which shouldn't be ignored.

Middlesbrough midfielder Sebastian Berhalter said: 'He's meant so much to me and he's helped me develop as a player and as a person. And as a player, that's all you can ask for, to have that trust and have that belief in you.'

But not every player in the system was tripping over themselves to play under Poch. Just ask Christian Pulisic, who took the entire summer off in 2025 to rest before the World Cup – only to put up a goose egg in his home country.

Any hope for further progress under Pochettino evaporated when United came calling

All of this being said, there was reason for hope in the future. By re-signing Pochettino, the chance to cement that work ethic, culture and leadership presented itself.

With his extension, Pochettino had the chance to build a foundation in US Soccer to engender future success for decades to come.

Now, that's all gone. Now, Pochettino's time in charge will be remembered more for unfulfilled potential than culture shifting. After all, how do you expect to keep a culture if its chief architect leaves?

US Soccer now is faced with a quagmire of either hiring the biggest possible name again (Guardiola, if you believe the rumors) or hiring someone who will treat the position less like a stepping stone and more like a cornerstone.

It never seemed like Pochettino fully embraced the US, despite the tears on Friday. He'll be off for Old Trafford and a United squad bogged down by perpetual disappointment, all while leaving behind the biggest "What If" in the still-growing history of the American game.

#1359. Engineered bacteria are weaning farms away from synthetic fertilizers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

Scientists are engineering bacteria that can provide nitrogen, an essential ingredient for plant growth, to wheat crops. Credit: Shakeel Ahmed/Anadolu Agency/Getty

The world’s farms depend on synthetic nitrogen fertilizers to increase crop yields, but the production and use of these chemicals generates billions of tonnes of greenhouse-gas emissions every year. Now, scientists are making progress on a greener alternative: bioengineered bacteria.

This approach takes a cue from natural bacteria that ‘fix’ nitrogen into a useful form and provide it to certain plants. Scientists are engineering genetic features into bacteria with the aim of enabling them to fix nitrogen for important food crops, such as maize (corn) and wheat, that don’t have such natural microbial partners.

In a comment published on 10 November in Nature Biotechnology1, researchers suggest that bioengineered bacteria could eventually replace up to half of synthetic fertilizers. The bacteria deliver nitrogen more efficiently to roots than synthetic fertilizers do, which could reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and nitrogen pollution of waterways. But this would require a slew of advances, from getting different microbial species to work together to more-rigorous field trials.

How CRISPR could yield the next blockbuster cropSome of these ‘biofertilizers’ have been augmented with genes and genetic snippets from viruses or distantly related bacteria. This means that the engineered microbes are classified as transgenic — altered to include DNA from other species. The bacteria are now being trialled on small plots of maize on farms in the Midwestern United States. The bacteria, developed by Switch Bioworks in San Carlos, California, are the first example of a transgenic biofertilizer approved for testing on fields in the country.

How CRISPR could yield the next blockbuster crop

In September, Switch Bioworks received approval from the Brazilian regulatory agency, the National Technical Commission on Biosafety (CNTBio), to test its strains there. This is the first time that a transgenic bacterium of any kind has been approved for field tests in Brazil, says molecular biologist Mario Murakami, who is the president of CTNBio in Campinas.

Companies that have focused on editing bacterial genes rather than producing transgenic microbes are further along. Pivot Bio in Minneapolis, Minnesota, has applied its gene-edited biofertilizers to tens of millions of hectares of US farmland over the past decade, says the company’s chief technology officer Travis Frey. Some of Pivot Bio’s products have also been tested in Canada, Argentina, Kenya and Brazil.

Most plants can’t use the form of nitrogen that is present in the air. Some crops, including soya beans and peanuts, host colonies of bacteria that can convert atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form. The plant takes up that nitrogen and, in return, provides carbon that fuels bacterial growth. But most staple crops lack these microbial partners, leading farmers to rely on synthetic nitrogen fertilizers. These chemical fertilizers account for 5% of global greenhouse-gas emissions, and drive damaging nutrient pollution in waterways.

For decades, researchers have tried to get bacteria to fix nitrogen for staple crops. Until recently, the approach was to collect wild strains of nitrogen-fixing bacteria from soil and apply them to seeds or spray them onto plants. “It doesn’t work,” says Jean-Michel Ané, a bioengineer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, who is working on microbial fertilizers. The wild microbes fail to thrive when applied to crops that don’t provide them with carbon.

How to climate-proof crops: scientists say the secret’s in the dirt

#1358. Declan Rice bites back at Graeme Souness: Arsenal star claims pundit doesn't understand how the game has evolved over 'old man's football' criticism - and jokes: 'My numbers aren't bad "for a centre-back!"'

Published: 15:30 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 15:40 EST, 14 November 2026

Declan Rice has laughed off criticism from Graeme Souness by claiming his numbers 'aren't bad for a centre back', after he was accused of playing 'old man's football' and 'cheating' by dropping into defence.

Souness has long believed the Arsenal and England star does not do enough for a midfielder and said recently he might as well play centre back, adding that he would not get a game for the likes of Real Madrid and Barcelona.

Rice is aware of what Souness has said but believes his return of 22 goals and 33 assists since joining the Gunners in 2023 disproves the former Liverpool midfielder's opinion.

‘My numbers since I joined Arsenal speak for themselves,’ said Rice. ‘For a “centre back”, I think that’s not bad numbers. I’ve had a lot of assists, a lot of goals. To be a top-class centre back getting those numbers, I’m delighted with that!’

Rice, who will start as an advanced midfielder when England take on Spain here in Madrid on Sunday night, added: ‘Look, Graeme’s got his opinion. I think he’s had his opinion since my West Ham days. I’ve seen his views. I can’t change his opinion. I can only do what I do, which is go on the pitch, perform, play well and block out the noise.’

Rice also believes Souness, 73, may not understand how the game has evolved.

England and Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice has laughed off Graeme Souness' criticism after he was accused of playing 'old man's football' 'cheating' by dropping into defence

Pundit Souness believes Rice would not get a game for the likes of Real Madrid and Barcelona

‘If you speak about the positioning, the “old man's football”, look at Harry Kane, for instance,’ began Rice. 'We played him the other week and he dropped next to the centre backs 20-30 times to pick up the ball. The game is different now. It's what the game demands, to get away from your man, to go into different areas to create overloads, to create two v ones, to progress the ball up the pitch. Football is way different. It's changed a lot, and you're always trying to look for tactical advantages.

‘In terms of me as a midfielder, I'm constantly watching clips with Mikel (Arteta). He's constantly coaching me on the pitch. How I can progress the ball from deep, drop next to the goalkeeper, go to full back to get on the ball, to take the ball up the pitch.

‘So, I feel like we're now seeing something totally different to what he would see, but in his time football was different. He was a top-class midfielder who won lots of stuff. There's no argument against him. As a pundit, as a person, his career, you have to respect what he's done.

‘I didn't get to see him play, but obviously his accolades were top, and I've never got to meet him in person. If I did, there would be no disrespect. I’d shake his hand. I’d chat with him. It’s an opinion at the end of the day. It’s football.’

#1356. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. “And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1355. Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision with Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel given 12-MATCH ban - and may never return to football

Published: 16:25 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 16:42 EST, 14 November 2026

The goalkeeper involved in the collision that killed Spanish footballer Jesus de Miguel has been hit with a 12-match ban - but may never play again.

FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been sanctioned after a horrifying foul with Tenerife's De Miguel earlier this month.

Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned with De Miguel, 30, admitted to intensive care, where he later died.

The goalkeeper was subjected to chants of 'murderer' by Tenerife supporters and retreated from public view amid the significant backlash.

Now his manager Carles Manso has said: 'We will ​give him space so that he feels completely free to make ‌any ⁠decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return.

'When he feels it is appropriate and when ​he feels genuinely ready to take a ​decision ⁠like that [he will do so].

Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been banned for 12 games and could quit football for good after he collided with Tenerife's Jesus De Miguel, who died

The striker was struck in the chest by Owono's flying knee as the keeper attempted to clear the ball near the halfway line

De Miguel was rushed to hospital following the incident after appearing motionless on the pitch

'What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to ​him.'

Earlier this month, Owono issued a statement describing his 'enormous pain' following the tragic on-field collision.

Owono said: 'These are being the most difficult days of my life. I am struggling to find the words and find it very difficult to assimilate anything that has happened.

'I feel an enormous pain for the loss of Jesús. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address; I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.

'But right now, honestly, I cannot think of anything else except Jesús and the pain we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesus.'

The tragedy occurred as the game entered the seventh minute of stoppage time, when De Miguel looked set to race away on the counter-attack for Tenerife in search of a winner.

As he watched a long ball drop into his path, the striker was struck in the chest by Owono's flying knee as he attempted to clear the ball near the halfway line.

After initially rolling around on the floor, De Miguel became motionless, and medical staff rushed onto the pitch to attend to him.

Police are investigating the death of De Miguel due to protocol, and they are also now probing the emergency medical response

Owono said he could not 'think of anything else except Jesús and the pain we are experiencing' (Source: Instagram/Jesus Owono)

Tenerife striker De Miguel died in the morning following the horrifying clash with Owono

Owono was initially given a red card for the challenge before the decision was soon taken by the referee to abandon the fixture.

De Miguel was seen to for over five minutes while his team-mates were visibly distressed, with some appearing to be in tears.

The stadium had been in complete silence while De Miguel was being treated, but as he was taken off the pitch the striker was given a standing ovation by the crowd.

He had become a father just last year, and according to El Espanol, his wife and baby daughter were watching in the stands as the fatal incident occurred.

After being taken to an ambulance on a stretcher, there is believed to have been an approximate 15-minute wait before they made their way to the hospital.

De Miguel is believed to have suffered a cardiac arrest while being transported to hospital and had to be revived inside the ambulance, according to Spanish media outlet Marca.

Spanish newspaper AS reported that De Miguel's team-mates had travelled to hospital after he had been taken to intensive care.

In a statement, CD Tenerife confirmed the striker's death, saying: 'Broken with pain, with a lump in our throat and unable to believe that this is true, from CD Tenerife we communicate the tragic death, this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8:00 a.m., of Jesus de Miguel Alameda.'

Tenerife stated: 'We are with his devastated family, with his loved ones, with all the people of Tenerife who today mourn this cruel outcome'

'There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing to mitigate this feeling full of sadness.

'We are with his devastated family, with his loved ones, with all the people of Tenerife who today mourn this cruel outcome.

#1354. Author or just ‘acknowledged’? How women are not gaining full credit for research

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Anna Napolitano is a freelance journalist in London.

The number of men with high citation counts exceeds that of women.Credit: FotografiaBasica/iStock via Getty

Women are more frequently mentioned in the acknowledgements section of papers than credited as co-authors, especially for research and analytical work, a study has found. But status seems to trump gender.

An analysis of more than 20,000 authors and 60,000 acknowledged contributors on papers published in seven PLOS journals between 2016 and 2021 highlighted persistent disparities between women and men in who gets authorship over an acknowledgement.

The study, published in Scientometrics1, also found that highly cited researchers — used by the authors as a proxy for higher status — were more likely to receive authorship over acknowledgement than were their less-cited collaborators, irrespective of gender. When a highly cited woman collaborated with a less-cited man, for example, the woman was more likely to be credited as an author.

Authorship is one of the most important metrics in research evaluation, grant reviews and promotion decisions, whereas acknowledgements aren’t typically factored in. The difference between getting authorship credit versus an acknowledgement can make or break a researcher’s career. One famous example is chemist Rosalind Franklin, a key contributor to the discovery of the DNA double helix. Franklin was mentioned in the acknowledgements section of the 1953 paper describing the finding, which went on to win the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, rather than being named a co-author with James Watson and Francis Crick.

The Scientometrics study highlights the importance of status in determining who gets credit, and the uphill battle that many women in research have to face — especially in their early and mid-careers. The number of highly cited men exceeded that of women, suggesting that even if women benefit from high status once they have attained it, fewer women attain higher status in the first place.

“We realized that the issue is double. One linked with gender bias, but another surprisingly due to hierarchy bias,” says Yukie Sano, a computational scientist at the University of Tsukuba in Japan, who co-authored the paper.

The impact of a researcher’s status and gender on academic credit is well-documented, but Sano and her co-authors point to the Contributor Role Taxonomy (CRediT) — a standardized system describing specific roles that individual scientists often take on during research — as a game-changer by providing high-quality data to track this metric across journals and disciplines.

Sano and her colleagues used CRediT data from open-access PLOS journals (which implemented the system in 2016) to track the contributions of authors and devised a separate system to track contributions in the acknowledgements section. Author gender was determined using Gender API, an artificial-intelligence-powered service that infers a person’s gender on the basis of their name.

The team found that men were generally more likely than women to receive authorship credit — particularly in investigation roles (performing the experiments) and analysis roles (analysing or synthesizing the study data). Around 70% of men were credited as authors, compared with about 65% of women.

The size of the gender gap varied between disciplines, but was particularly evident in medicine, biology and computer science, whereas environmental science showed little evidence of a gender difference in authorship versus acknowledgement rates.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03448-7

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. #1351. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

But the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Despite losing Danny Welbeck, last year’s top scorer, Brighton have scored 23 goals already this Premier League campaign, the most in the league. This tally includes one of the most extraordinary goals in Premier League history.

Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Receiving a short pass from Olivier Boscagli just inside his own half, Gómez could have sought to pick out a team-mate. Instead, his scanning of the pitch before receiving the ball had revealed that goalkeeper Walter Benítez was off his line and Brighton’s attacking players were being tightly guarded by defenders. And so, just as he entered the centre circle in the opposition half, Gómez attempted the absurd.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.
