#1313. Inside Sir Alex Ferguson's inner circle of Man United legends: The player threatened 'he will end up in a ditch' by football chief, the cult-hero striker still playing at 38 and sorry Michael Carrick after his Old Trafford sacking

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 02:01 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 11:52 EST, 15 November 2026

It's safe to say Manchester United are going through a rough patch - and then some - at the moment, but many of their supporters would have raised a smile at one photo that surfaced earlier this month.

A few of the club's legends reunited to raise a glass to Sir Alex Ferguson on his 40th anniversary of being named Red Devils manager.

Ferguson, who retired in 2013, won 38 major honours during a trophy-laden 26 years at Old Trafford.

And as the 84-year-old received plaudits across the footballing world, he enjoyed a celebratory intimate setting with some of his former players and actor James Nesbitt in Manchester.

Diehard United fan Nesbitt shared a group photo on Instagram, featuring Ferguson alongside Michael Carrick, Edwin van der Sar, Nemanja Vidic, Robin van Persie, Darren Fletcher, Jonny Evans, Javier Hernandez and John O'Shea.

But what are those former United players up to now? Daily Mail Sport takes a look...

Actor and Man United fan James Nesbitt (centre right) posted this picture with club royalty - clockwise from front left: Jonny Evans, Darren Fletcher, Robin van Persie, Nemanja Vidic, Michael Carrick, John O'Shea, Sir Alex Ferguson, Edwin van der Sar and Javier Hernandez

Unless you've been on another planet, then you would know everything about Carrick this past week.

The 45-year-old was sacked as United head coach on Thursday morning after a disastrous start to the season.

Carrick, who has been replaced by Mauricio Pochettino, oversaw United's worst top-flight start since Ferguson replaced Ron Atkinson 40 years ago - with one victory in 10 Premier League matches as they sit 18th.

Furthermore this season, he only won three of 15 games in all competitions.

The downturn in the Red Devils' form is bewildering considering their upturn when Carrick replaced Ruben Amorim in mid-January last season. He was handed a two-year contract in May after guiding United to a third-place finish and qualification for the Champions League, losing just two of his 17 games as head coach.

Carrick was sacked as Manchester United head coach on Thursday morning by club chiefs

He oversaw United's worst top-flight start in Premier League history with one win in 10 games

Like Carrick, Evans is also out of a job having been part of his backroom staff at United as first-team coach.

After retiring as a player at the end of the 2024-25 season, Evans took up the position of head of loans and pathways at Carrington but left that role last December.

Following Amorim's sacking he returned to the club to help Fletcher during his caretaker manager stint before being kept on by Carrick.

Like Carrick, Evans was relieved of his United duties having been part of his backroom team

The sole former player still connected directly with the club, Fletcher is their Under 18s head coach. The Scot had to pause his role last season when becoming the club's first-team interim head coach following Amorim's sacking in January - drawing 2-2 with Burnley in the Premier League before overseeing their FA Cup third-round home defeat by Brighton a few days later.

Having come through the club's academy, Fletcher knows what it takes to make the grade at the club and has the likes of Kai Rooney, son of Wayne, and Jacey Carrick, son of Michael, among his squad.

And Fletcher's young charges are enjoying a strong start to the season which has included six goals in wins over Liverpool (6-3) and Burnley (6-0) at the end of last month.

Fletcher is the Red Devils' U18s head coach - nurturing the club's latest crop of rising stars

The former Red Devils captain had ambitions to go into coaching, having done his badges, but has turned his focus on building up a real estate portfolio - telling Gary Neville on The Overlap last July that he had put £4.5million into building 76 one or two-bedroom apartments in Belgrade, Serbia.

However, this summer it was reported that Vidic had been a previous target of intimidation by a former football chief.

According to Serbian media, encrypted messages show then-Serbia's football president Slavisa Kokeza wanted people to threaten Vidic after he had publicly criticised the Serbian Football Association (FSS) over the national side's failure to qualify for the Euro 2020 tournament.

In the reported devised plot in 2020, Kokeza reportedly told one contact to make it clear to Vidic that he should 'stay away from the association or he will end up in a ditch'.

As well as that, criminals were hired to monitor the former centre-back's movements in Milan, where he lived, and fit his car with a tracking device.

Following the revelations, Vidic and his legal team filed a criminal complaint and sought an investigation into the claimed plot.

'In mid-May, OCCRP and KRIK visited my home and told me they had obtained encrypted messages from Sky ECC (a now-defunct communication encryption service which EUROPOL said was widely used by criminals and was broken into by European police in 2021) and analysed them,' Vidic told The Athletic in July.

'The messages were said to have come from the then-president of the SFF in 2020. They were about me and how to stop me from talking to the media. At the time, I was commentating on the situation in Serbian football. I was living in Milan, Italy, where I stayed after finishing my career with Inter. I hadn't yet moved back to Serbia, where I am from and where I live.'

Vidic, who has turned his focus on building up a real estate portfolio, was reportedly a previous target of intimidation by a former football chief

Van der Sar's calm persona on the football pitch translated well into the boardroom during his near-seven-year stint at Ajax as their chief executive officer.

The former Manchester United goalkeeper joined the Dutch giants' board in 2012, becoming CEO in 2016. During his spell Ajax reached the 2017 Europa League final and 2019 Champions League semi-finals with a young exciting core of players including the likes of Frenkie de Jong and Matthijs de Ligt.

The year Van der Sar left though Ajax finished third that season to qualify for the Europa League play-offs, missing out on the Champions League for the first time since 2009.

A few weeks later in July 2023, Van der Sar was put in intensive care after suffering a brain haemorrhage while on holiday in Croatia.

Three years on since recovering, Van der Sar is enjoying being away from football for the time being telling The Overlap in February: 'Now it's almost three years ago, so I've had time to recover with no stress, no phone in my hand - just doing the stuff that I've wanted to do.

'Wake up when you want, walk the dog, go swim in the sea, go on holiday. I went to New Zealand for two months with [wife] Annemarie - nice things that I never had the chance to do before.

'I started playing at 18 or 19, finished at 40, and at 41 I became one of the directors at Ajax until 53, so I thought it was the right time to take a step back. That's taken a little bit longer than I originally thought, to be fair, but we are enjoying ourselves very much.'

Van der Sar was Ajax CEO for seven years before stepping down from the role in 2023

The ex-goalkeeper is now enjoying life with wife Annemarie after a brain haemorrhage in 2023

Like Carrick, Van Persie has turned his hand to first-team management since retiring.

His first role was with Dutch outfit Heerenveen - signing a two-year contract with the club ahead of the 2024-25 season. However, his time there lasted just nine months as he took over the reins at Dutch giants Feyenoord.

However, his time in Rotterdam lasted just 16 months there when he was sacked in June. He had guided them to second in the Eredivisie but they finished 19 points behind champions PSV Eindhoven.

In explaining his sacking, newly-appointed technical director Devy Rigaux cited the style of play as a factor.

'We conducted a thorough internal analysis,' he said. 'In this, we took into account, among other things, the development of the style of play and the declining trend in terms of points total, both in Europe and in the Eredivisie.

'The conclusion was that it is better to start the next season with a new head coach.'

The 43-year-old is awaiting a new job, like Carrick.

Van Persie is currently without a managerial job after being sacked by Feyenoord in June

The sole player from this list to still be playing, Hernandez made history by becoming the first-ever player signed to USL Championship outfit Atletico Dallas.

In July, the 38-year-old penned a two-year deal with an option for a third year at the expansion club which will play in the second-tier of US football, below Major League Soccer.

The Mexican striker still has a few months to wait for his debut though, with the season not beginning until March 2027.

In the meantime, he was part of the FOX broadcast team for the recent World Cup in the United States, Mexico and Canada, serving as an analyst.

Last year, Hernandez was caught up in a sexism storm, which he later apologised for, after he made a series of statements on TikTok 'promoting sexist stereotypes that are considered media violence and go against gender equality in sport'.

Hernandez said women are 'failing' and 'eradicating masculinity'.

'Don't be afraid to be women, to allow yourselves to be led by a man,' said the former Mexico captain on social media.

His remarks sparked a backlash, which led to his apology which included him saying: 'I deeply regret any confusion or discomfort that my recent words have caused.'

Hernandez was fined and warned about his future conduct.

Hernandez, who attended United's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on November 8, is the only player still playing and has signed for USL Championship outfit Atletico Dallas ahead of their new term

Like the majority of the names here, O'Shea's post-playing career has seen him turn to coaching with his current role being the Republic of Ireland assistant head coach.

The 45-year-old has been in this position since August 2024, staying on with his homeland's setup following the appointment of Heimir Hallgrimsson as manager.

O'Shea took charge of the team for four friendly fixtures that year following Stephen Kenny's departure in November 2023. His record read one win, one draw and two defeats in that period.

The former defender will be hoping to help his country qualify for Euro 2028 which will be played on home soil across the Republic of Ireland, England, Scotland and Wales.

O'Shea is Republic of Ireland assistant head coach - a role he has held since August 2024

#1312. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

Emery had warned his players of complacency against the Norwegian champions, but Villa took command from the start and were ahead after 23 minutes.

Ross Barkley scored twice against Fenerbahce last week and was in the right place again to head Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner past Arild Ostbo.

#1311. Pochettino Must Make Lewis Hall First Man Utd Signing After 10/10 Display

Now Mauricio Pochettino has been confirmed as the new Manchester United manager, attentions are already turning to who could follow him to Old Trafford during the January transfer window.

Fabrizio Romano has already confirmed that Man United are expected to make at least one signing in the New Year, and it could even be more depending on the opportunities available to them, with centre-back and striker seen as two priority positions for the winter market.

Until then, Pochettino must work with the players he has, and he will be looking to pick up the win needed to take the Red Devils out of the Premier League relegation zone when they face rivals Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday in his first match in charge.

The Argentine won't have too long to work with his players on the training ground ahead of the trip to Merseyside, and he will be hoping to have some of his experienced players available to face Andoni Iraola's men.

There is currently a chance that the likes of Marcus Rashford, who Pochettino is said to love, Harry Maguire and Luke Shaw could be fit to face the Reds after fitness issues.

The left-back position was a big problem for Carrick in the latter stages of his reign at Old Trafford, with Shaw's absence seeing the 45-year-old use Patrick Dorgu and also Diogo Dalot there out of position, as United struggled majorly from a defensive point of view.

The position was one that United wanted to strengthen during the summer window, but they were unable to find the right deal and instead focused their attentions on signing three central midfield players.

They would have hoped that would have been a safe decision after Shaw played all 38 Premier League matches last term, but his injury issues have surfaced again to cause the Red Devils problems.

One of United's key left-back targets during the summer window was Newcastle United star Lewis Hall, and he looks to be the perfect long-term replacement for Luke Shaw at Old Trafford.

Hall's price tag and the fact that they had already sold Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes during the summer made a deal impossible, before the 22-year-old signed a new five-year deal to extend his stay at St James' Park.

That could make any move for Hall even more difficult, but he produced a reminder of why he would be the perfect signing for United during England's brilliant 3-2 win against Spain on Sunday night.

Pochettino loved Shaw's attributes as a young left-back at Southampton, and Hall continues to display the same traits as he continues to establish himself as one of the best young left-backs in Europe.

England's full-backs were both outstanding in Madrid as Thomas Tuchel's men produced one of their best wins in years, ending Spain's 43-match unbeaten run as a result.

Hall was up against Lamine Yamal in the Metropolitano Stadium, but he dealt with the Barcelona star with ease, also providing a big threat from an attacking point of view too.

Those are the exact traits Pochettino wants from his full-backs, and the Magpies star was labelled 'world-class' and handed a 10/10 rating by talkSPORT pundit Adrian Durham for his performance in the Spanish capital.

If United really intend to make big strides under the Argentine manager, they need to make another big investment in their defence in 2027, and Hall should be their number-one left-back target.

Newcastle may see Hall as a player worth around £100m now, having sold Tonali for a similar fee to Tottenham, but that shouldn't dissuade the Red Devils' hierarchy moving for a player who can be their left-back for many years.

#1309. To Fund Nusa: Arsenal Must Sell Zubimendi in January After England Disaster

Arsenal are expected to make a move or two in the January transfer window, as they look to bolster Mikel Arteta's attacking options ahead of the second half of the season.

The Gunners have enjoyed an impressive start to the new campaign, winning nine of their first ten Premier League matches, whilst conceding just five goals in the process. However, Arteta's side have only scored 15 goals, and thus, there is a recognition from the Premier League champions' coaching staff and hierarchy that they need more offensive firepower to get them over the line later in the season.

Antonio Nusa has been heavily linked with a switch to North London, with Arsenal reportedly weighing up a potential move for the Norwegian. Nusa has scored six goals and provided eight assists in 15 appearances already this season for RB Leipzig, so the German club are unlikely to sanction his departure mid-way through the campaign for a bargain.

Arsenal will likely need to fork out a substantial sum to get their hands on the 21-year-old, and they may even need to sell a player or two to raise funds and create squad space for the player to arrive.

Nusa' Statistics 2026/27 (Bundesliga Only)

Several Gunners players could be considered for a sale, although there is one who is particularly vulnerable in Arteta's squad at the moment.

After a largely impressive debut season in English football faded out due to fatigue, Martin Zubimendi has been relegated to the periphery of Arteta's squad this term.

The Spaniard finds himself behind the likes of Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Mikel Merino in the pecking order at the Emirates, sparking speculation that he could be on his way out in January.

This uncertainty surrounding his future appears to have affected the midfielder, whose form shows no signs of improving his standing in the Arsenal squad.

Starting in midfield for Spain against England on Sunday evening, Zubimendi had an opportunity to remind the world of the levels he can show. He failed to do so.

Hooked with 20 minutes left with an injury, Spanish media were not happy with the former Real Sociedad man's contributions.

Marca argued that Zubimendi was 'nowhere to be seen' on the night, while AS described the player's showing as 'disastrous'.

"His second consecutive appearance as Rodri's replacement was a disastrous night for him. He struggled to control the game against [Declan] Rice's aggressive marking, suffering several dangerous turnovers and rarely finding the Spanish second-to-last line of defense. To make matters worse, he had to leave the field injured in the 71st minute." - Marca on Zubimendi vs England

Given his paucity of minutes currently at Arsenal, a below-par display against England could be detrimental to Zubimendi's chances of rediscovering his important role in North London.

With Zubimendi looking somewhat redundant in Arsenal's squad, it makes sense for the Gunners to cash in on him in January whilst he still has an extensive list of suitors. Atletico Madrid, Real Madrid and Chelsea are all said to be interested in landing the 27-year-old.

While he might generate in excess of £50 million, which can go towards signing Nusa, his departure would also make sense regarding the Norway international's arrival, from a pure squad-building standpoint.

The Atletico Madrid star was desperate to leave in the summer, but was unable to secure a move.

Eberechi Eze has so far been used primarily as a left-winger this season by Arteta. If Zubimendi leaves, the Englishman will be moved centrally again, creating a spot in the squad for a new left-sided forward.

The jigsaw pieces fit, while the finances also make sense. Zubimendi is doing very little with his performances to quieten the noise around a potential exit, and the convenience around the potential deal makes it too difficult for Arsenal to ignore this winter.

#1308. Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli needs a statement win to change the narrative around his new-look side

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 13:37 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 13:37 EST, 15 November 2026

While it’s fair to state that the touchpaper has yet to be lit on Sebastien Pocognoli’s tenure, he is hardly the first Scotland manager to discover that the battle for hearts and minds can be a drawn-out affair.

Although Steve Clarke marked the start of his era with an unconvincing win over Cyprus at Hampden in 2019, the Ayrshireman lost his next four games to Russia and Belgium. It would take him 15 months to chalk up what might be considered a statement victory.

That 2-1 win against the Czech Republic in Olomouc in September 2020, in his tenth match in charge, felt like a turning point for the national team and so it proved with qualification for the delayed Euros in the post. But Clarke certainly had to suffer for it.

So for all the frustration felt at Pocognoli’s new-look side failing to hit the straps in the past five matches, we have been here before. And statistically, to date, it’s also been by no means disastrous.

Notwithstanding how ordinary North Macedonia are, the Belgian is actually the first manager since Gordon Strachan in 2013 to win more than one of his first five games in charge. The history books show that Scotland don’t really do fast starts when there’s a new man at the helm.

Nonetheless, it would be hard to overstate the significance of Pocognoli seeing it all spectacularly come together as the Nations League campaign concludes in St Gallen tomorrow.

Scotland captain Andy Robertson and John McGinn enjoy a light-hearted moment in training.

Sebastien Pocognoli is one of many Scotland managers who have made slow starts in the job.

Switzerland boss Murat Yakin will give some of his fringe players a chance against Scotland.

Friday’s win over the group whipping boys was certainly deserved, yet the performance, particularly in the first half, was hardly scintillating.

Even those who are prepared to be patient with Pocognoli would have been concerned at the lack of tempo and imagination in the general play in the first period.

Weren’t we told that he would bring a radically different approach to Clarke? Yet there was scant evidence on show of the ultra-offensive, high-pressing style which was billed in the brochure.

While a markedly better second half yielded a welcome first home win for the 39-year-old, no one left the arena clicking their heels at what they’d witnessed. This remains very much a work in progress.

What can be said with some certainty, however, is that the players are on board with the grand plan. When they faced the media last week, it was noticeable that Scott McTominay, Andy Robertson and John McGinn all praised the new man’s methods and ideas and predicted that they will bear fruit in the fullness of time.

You get a sense when experienced players are reading empty platitudes from a prepared script. Yet the words of the leadership group felt truly authentic on that occasion.

While Pocognoli will obviously have welcomed them, it’s not statements of support from senior figures which he needs to keep the Tartan Army onside. It’s positive results.

Come what may against Switzerland tomorrow, Scotland don’t have a match until March. That’s an awful long time to reflect if it doesn’t go well.

What Pocognoli and the travelling fans wouldn’t give for that seismic win to shift the narrative and engender a greater sense of optimism ahead of the Euro qualifiers.

Strachan’s first big scalp arrived at the fourth time of asking when a Robert Snodgrass goal sealed an unlikely win away to Croatia. Such unexpected outcomes can have a galvanising effect.

Friday’s narrow win over North Macedonia did keep the possibility alive of Scotland finishing second in Group B1, but few would be sticking their house on that yet coming to pass.

With head-to-head rather than goal difference counting if sides are locked on the same number of points, Pocognoli’s men must beat the Swiss then hope that Slovenia don’t win in Skopje. Stranger things have happened, but not too many.

In all likelihood, Scotland will finish third and be a pot three team when the draw for Euro 2028 is made in Belfast on December 6. Yet, it’s still vital that they conclude this campaign with – at the very least – a display which offers grounds for optimism.

This was always going to be the toughest assignment of the six. In the summer, the Swiss reached the last eight of the World Cup for the first time since 1954, only losing in extra-time to Argentina. That remains their only defeat this year.

They’ve hardly missed a beat in the Nations League, winning four games and drawing one, to comfortably secure promotion to the top tier.

Even though they were given a helping hand by Jack Hendry’s early red card as they won 3-0 at Hampden in September, they looked a level above Pocognoli’s men.

‘We reached all of our goals,’ said coach Murat Yakin.

‘Maybe we could have done even more at the World Cup, but we created history by reaching the quarter-finals.

‘I am happy with our playing style. There’s been good development and we have integrated new players.’

The hope for Scotland stems from the fact that Yakin is compelled to give some fringe players an opportunity to shine in St Gallen.

Inter Milan’s Manuel Akanji has become the latest big name to withdraw through injury. Johan Manzambi, Dan Ndoye and Granit Xhaka were already out.

Even then, the task for the visitors remains formidable. The only defeat for the Swiss in their past 11 games on home soil came at the hands of Germany.

‘It has happened a few times already,’ Yakin said of the injury situation.

‘But we will make sure we get a good level of players on to the pitch. It’s a good thing we have won the group already. It’s now an opportunity to make changes.

‘It doesn’t make sense to wait. We have enough opportunities and possibilities.’

It feels like a night for Pocognoli to proceed with caution. A fairly assured display against North Macedonia means Ryan Porteous, Luke Graham and Kieran Tierney will probably be asked to go again as a back-three.

Given his defensive diligence, Aaron Hickey would be favoured to displace Ben Gannon-Doak on the right flank.

As on Friday, Billy Gilmour and Lewis Ferguson should play behind John McGinn and Scott McTominay with Che Adams leading the line.

On the occasion when he’ll become Scotland’s most capped player with 103 appearances, it’s to be hoped Andy Robertson has a night to remember.

‘What can I say about him?’ added Yakin. ‘He’s a fantastic player, who has also constantly carried the team or the nation of Scotland.

‘The best players should be on the pitch and we’re happy to compete with him. It’s a nice mark for him, and in that sense, congratulations.’

#1307. How I balance my life as a professional surfer and a university researcher

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Cliff Kapono is a professional surfer and marine conservation scientist.

Cliff Kapono enjoys professional surfing as an adjunct to his academic career. Credit: Nani Welch Keliihoomalu for Nature

During my graduate studies at the University of California, San Diego, long hours in the laboratory were often stressful, and not just because of the research. Most of my anxiety came from looking out the window at perfect surfing conditions and realizing I didn’t have much time to finish my experiments and leave while the ‘waves were firing’.

Several years on, I am now an assistant professor at the School of Ocean Futures at Arizona State University (ASU), working from Hilo, Hawaii, where I balance scientific research with my second job: travelling the world as a non-competitive professional surfer. Also known as a free surfer, I ride a variety of board designs — from conventional wooden surfboards to modern big-wave ‘guns’ — and produce social-media content, such as photos and videos, in exchange for endorsement opportunities.

My research is also deeply connected to the ocean. I study coral microbiomes, sampling the community of microorganisms living on and in the coral before and after environmental stress to improve understanding of reef health and the sea-bed formations that create waves, referred to as surf breaks. In May, my colleagues and I reported on the importance of creating a framework to analyse systems with environmental, social and cultural components to protect surf ecosystems1.

In my faculty position, I work in nine-month appointments, and I am permitted to spend a number of work hours each calendar year on non-conflicting outside business. I spend roughly 85% of my work year on research and teaching and 15% on surfing assignments.

Many careers are no longer confined to a single discipline or identity, and some of the most meaningful work now happens at the intersection between different skills, communities and ways of thinking. Surfing shapes the questions I want to ask as a scientist, while science provides me with ways to understand and protect ocean environments. When I was a student, I used to worry that I would have to choose between surfing and science. Today, my career exists because I didn’t.

When I graduated from high school in 2005, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders made up less than 0.2% of all science, technology, engineering and mathematics degree graduates in the United States. Today, that number remains at only 0.3%2. As a Native Hawaiian kid, targeted fellowships and private programmes made university possible for me, covering my tuition and board.

After I started a PhD chemistry programme at the University of California, San Diego, in 2012, my studies became much more demanding. Courses, a teaching-assistant role, fellowship requirements and lab training would keep me on land from sunrise until sundown. Despite being able to see the ocean from nearly every window on campus, it was the time in my life that I felt furthest from it.

Remarkably, it was during the third year of my PhD programme that getting paid to surf actually became a reality. After many nights spent in the lab, I decided to set academic boundaries and rededicate time to the waves, mostly as a way to protect my mental health. I stopped measuring success only by hours in the lab. Instead, I treated time in the ocean as part of the scientific process.

Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?

Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?

Surfing-industry figures took notice, and not long after becoming more present on the beaches, I was offered modest ambassadorial contracts that developed into respectable budgets that let me travel to places with better waves and to collaborate with local board builders — when not in the lab, of course.

When I moved back to Hawaii in 2018, I received a US National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellowship for broadening participation of under-represented groups in biology and I began to use surfing as a vehicle for communicating coral science. That eventually led to Arizona State University recruiting me to join its Hilo-based Center for Global Discovery and Conservation Science in 2021, a position that has since evolved into my current role.

Blending the two disciplines has made my research more creative and my surfing more meaningful. It also taught me the importance of protecting time for the parts of life that keep you grounded. Whether that be surfing, music, art or family, maintaining space for your passions is not a distraction from academic work; it is often the very thing that sustains it.

Here are some guiding principles that have helped me to navigate the worlds of surfing and academia.

The best experiences come when you find a crew that wants to surf the same waves or explore the same questions as you. Some of the most important opportunities in my career came from relationships that started organically, often through time spent in the ocean and local communities, or through a shared curiosity, rather than formal networking.

The researchers, surfers, photographers and conservationists I work with are people who genuinely care about the places we study and the communities connected to them. Over time, those shared values create trust that later opens doors to research projects, publications, funding opportunities and creative collaborations. I’ve found that the best way to find these people is not by chasing status or connections but by consistently showing up in the communities and places that you genuinely care about.

#1306. Donnarumma: ‘Italy paid for exhilarating France win, nobody expected this run’

Gianluigi Donnarumma feels Italy were carrying a hangover from the ‘exhilarating’ victory over France, but the 4-1 defeat to Belgium mustn’t wipe out their other Nations League performances.

The Manchester City goalkeeper was one of the best Azzurri performers on the night in Brussels, managing to keep the scoreline down to only 4-1, especially with some incredible saves on Kevin De Bruyne.

Pio Esposito had opened the scoring, yet Maxim De Cuyper, Nathan Ngoy, Jeremy Doku and Diego Moreira turned it all around, with Senne Lammens saving the late Esposito spot-kick too.

“Unfortunately, this is part of the learning process, we started a new era, so you can have these ups and downs,” Donnarumma told RAI Sport.

It was hard to see this performance just days after the 3-1 comeback victory over France at San Siro, which put Italy temporarily top of the Nations League group.

“We weren’t phenomenal then and we’re not a disaster now. It was a wonderful night with France, and perhaps we used up too much energy to achieve that result, so were a little tired just three days later.

“When you play a match that is so exhilarating, it’s not easy to plug straight back in at the same level. It’s not an excuse, but we were certainly less sharp than the other day,” continued Donnarumma.

“Let’s be honest, nobody expected us to have such a good Nations League campaign, we had some really impressive matches, but Belgium were superior tonight, and we know that we must improve.”

Italy only needed a point in Brussels to secure qualification for the quarter-finals, so Belgium expected them to take a defensive approach and play for the draw, but that certainly was not the case.

“What we need to reflect on is that we allowed so many counter-attacks, so we must do better with the preventative marking,” noted Donnarumma.

“This defeat can and will be a valuable learning experience, the coach already said we need to lift our heads. It was painful, we all wanted to keep going in this tournament.”

Roberto Mancini is certainly trying to widen the group of players he can call upon for Italy, as this evening Milan winger Alphadjo Cisse received his senior debut, while Roma’s Niccolò Pisilli got his first competitive start.

“The coach is special, he can give us a big hand. We too have to help the younger players, and we know there isn’t much time because the European Championship qualifiers are coming up, but they need to play and gain experience.

“There are many interesting young players out there, but they need to play more often.”

Please stop with the excuses… we Italians often do this. Is our captain saying beating France is the reason why we lost today?

“The Manchester City goalkeeper was one of the best Azzurri performers”

#1305. Man City: Lawyers Rate Chances of Successful Appeal Against 114 Charges

Manchester City are facing an anxious wait to discover the outcome of their appeal after being found guilty on 114 financial charges.

The Citizens were accused of artificially inflating sponsorship deals using 'sham' contracts and other methods, with the Premier League's investigation starting in 2023.

In September 2026, the club were found guilty on 114 charges before launching an appeal shortly after. The outcome of that process is still undecided as the legal battle continues.

A report from the Financial Times has claimed that City's hearing is set to take place in December and could take place over several days.

As a result, the outcome is expected in the New Year, with sanctions handed out at the same time if Man City fail to overturn the guilty verdict. David Kogan, the head of the Independent Football Regulator, backed up that information.

Now, football financial expert Nick Harris has shed light on what legal experts think will happen. He has covered the entire case and has spoken with several lawyers throughout.

Manchester City's transfer plans are already being affected by their guilty verdict.

From those he's had conversations with, Harris reckons one in four think City will win parts of the appeal. However, even fewer are of the belief that their wins will be big enough.

He tweeted: "From multiple lawyers I’ve spoken to, perhaps 25% think City will win the appeal or parts of the appeal, but fewer think City will win substantive points. ie: will still lose.

"Context: on the morning of the 2016 US presidential election, Trump had a 26- 28% chance of winning (max). But he won."

If the guilty verdict sticks, attention will quickly turn to the players. Who will remain loyal to the club as they battle through whichever sanctions they are hit with?

Well, Harris revealed that Erling Haaland, City's main man, could be on his way to Real Madrid if the verdict isn't overturned. He posted on X:

"Florentino Perez is increasingly confident Erling Haaland will be a Real Madrid player next season, according to a contact who had lunch with Pérez recently. Meanwhile, multiple MCFC players' agents are exploring how their players might leave on free transfers if all City appeals fail. IF."

Haaland himself was asked about the charges during the international break. After playing for Norway, he said: "In 2009, I was playing for Bryne under-nine boys.

"This is a question I struggle to answer. It is a matter between the Premier League and Manchester City that is going to be dealt with by a panel. Am I supposed to answer that? I'm not really sure.

"It's a difficult question to answer when I don't really know that much about it. I assume the answers will come in the next ... I don't know when the answers will come. I haven't read that much about it."

#1304. Van Bommel: ‘Belgium would score six without Donnarumma, my advice to De Bruyne’

Mark van Bommel insists Belgium ‘would’ve scored six if not for Gianluigi Donnarumma’ in goal for Italy, and clarifies he never advised Kevin De Bruyne to quit Napoli for PSV Eindhoven.

This was an incredibly tight Nations League group, and going into the final match the Azzurri were on top with 10 points, ahead of France on goal difference and head-to-head record, with Belgium following on nine.

By the end of the night, Italy had dropped to third place following a 4-1 defeat in Brussels, despite taking the early lead through Pio Esposito.

The hosts had turned it around within 15 minutes to lead 3-1 with Maxim De Cuyper, Nathan Ngoy and Jeremy Doku, then Diego Moreira added a fourth on the classic counter-attack, while Senne Lammens saved Pio Esposito’s late penalty.

“If Donnarumma had not been in goal, then we would’ve scored six,” insisted Van Bommel to Sky Sport Italia.

It was a dominant performance, far more than the 2-0 victory at the Stadio Olimpico in the opening round of this Nations League group.

Curiously, Italy lost both matches with Belgium, while the Red Devils lost both meetings with France, yet the only team Les Bleus were unable to beat was the Azzurri.

“I’ll be honest, I didn’t expect this when we started two months ago, but even before that first match with Italy, I could tell this was a really intelligent group of players. That makes it a pleasure for a coach to work with them.”

De Bruyne’s performance this evening made him look a completely different player to the one seen regularly in Serie A and the Champions League at Napoli.

Considering the rumours that he is looking for a January transfer to PSV Eindhoven, has the Belgium coach given him any advice on the next step in his career?

“I was asked a question by a Belgian reporter about whether De Bruyne would fit in with the PSV Eindhoven style of play, and seeing as I know the club well, I said yes he would, but he also fits in at Napoli,” insisted Van Bommel.

“So I answered a specific question, but I did not advise him to do anything. The decision is entirely his, and I leave that to him.”

Former Napoli striker Romelu Lukaku remained on the bench throughout and was never deployed.

“He was injured for a few days and didn’t even make the trip to Turkiye, so tonight we said that we would use him in case of emergency. It was a bit cold as well, so we decided together not to bring him on.”

#1303. Tim Howard Blasted For 'Bonkers' Reaction to USA Wanting Guardiola to Replace Pochettino

James is a Senior Editor for GIVEMESPORT with over eight years of experience in the industry. After graduating from the University of Southampton in 2016 with a degree in history, he joined the company as an Academy member in July 2017 and, after a short time working as a freelancer, was given a full-time role in February 2018.  He primarily covers the biggest stories in the football world but is also comfortable reporting on a variety of other sports including darts, golf, Formula 1, tennis, boxing and athletics. He has covered some massive events during his time at GIVEMESPORT, including numerous Champions League and World Cup finals, as well as the Olympics in 2020 and 2024.

The United States Men's National Team are looking for a new manager after Mauricio Pochettino made the decision to leave his role and join Manchester United.

The Argentine was appointed USA manager in 2024. He has won 22 of his 36 matches in charge, leading his side to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup on home soil. He will manage the Stars and Stripes one final time against Haiti on Tuesday evening.

USA are aiming high as they search for a replacement for Pochettino. According to GiveMeSport sources, Pep Guardiola is on their radar, and they want him to be their manager.

Guardiola, considered one of the greatest managers in football history, is currently a free agent after leaving Manchester City in the summer.

It remains to be seen whether USA are able to land Guardiola, but many think that he would be an incredible coup should he put pen-to-paper.

USMNT legends Tim Howard and Landon Donovan don't share that opinion, though. Speaking on 'Unfiltered Soccer with Landon Donovan & Tim Howard', the pair explained why they thought the USA shouldn't go for Guardiola. Howard said:

"Pep Guardiola. And by the way, I think the next time I see Pep Guardiola, he might smack me and I'm okay with that. He's absolutely not the right manager for this team, for the length of time that it's going to take to get through to the next World Cup.

"Here's why. Pep Guardiola has only ever succeeded with tier-one players. People might get upset with this. We have probably tier-three players globally. Probably. I might have been a tier-three player myself, whatever.

"But Pep Guardiola, Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Man City with more money than probably should have, has succeeded. We actually, me, you and every other football fan in the world, we actually don't know if Pep Guardiola is a good manager. Coaching level two or three players, we do not know. We do not know. And nobody out there can tell me they know."

Donovan agreed with his compatriot, adding: "Pep is a phenomenal manager, but this would not be right for the U.S. team. Would he be good for our 18-year-old players? I don't know. We have good, elite players, but he's been with the best.

"Pep is a genius who changed the way soccer is played in the world, but that is way different from having two training sessions to prepare for Haiti this week.

"As a national team coach, being a manager of people is way more important than getting the team to play a certain way. I don't think he fits for us."

Their comments haven't gone down well among USMNT fans.

One said: ‘I cannot believe what I just heard.' A second commented: ‘What the heck did Howard actually say that?’ while a third stated: 'This is horrendous from both of them.'

A fourth commented: 'The dumbest thing I’ve ever heard and another reason USMNT will always be trash. If Pep even picks up the phone you’d be lucky.'

'Bonkers take. He is too good for us,' a fifth said, while a sixth wrote: 'They are so scared a USMNT might some day better than they were they actively are moving against the idea of hiring this generation's best manager.'

At the time of writing, Guardiola is the third favourite to replace Pochettino. Nashville SC boss BJ Callaghan is the leading contender.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Vincent Kompany is in the building. It wasn’t clear whether the Bayern head coach would be able to attend tonight’s game because he’s been battling a nasty virus over the last few days. He did not do the usual pre-match press conference yesterday but clearly feels well enough to be here tonight.

In an extract from Sam Dean’s new book on Arsenal’s resurgence under the Spaniard, he reveals that Mike Ashley was keen to bring Arteta to Newcastle United in 2019.

Arsenal: The Inside Story of Arsenal’s Rebirth Under Mikel Arteta (Pan Macmillan, RRP £22).

This is a proper heavyweight clash but, sadly for the neutrals watching, Bayern are missing some big players. Michael Olise is suspended, Jamal Musiala is injured and Joshua Kimmich is unavailable following the death of his father.

This should all work in Arsenal’s favour, and Mikel Arteta will be looking for a repeat of the energy and quality that his team showed against Bayern last season. Ice cold from Martinelli 🥶 https://t.co/uQEHb4x7eH

Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

#1301. Legendary commentator CLIVE TYLDESLEY on how his ITV exit has made hearts grow fonder, the rise of YouTube streamers, his lockdown money-spinner - and why he refuses to be another loud voice in the game

Published: 02:01 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 14:00 EST, 15 November 2026

Clive Tyldesley reaches for his glasses as he rummages through the commentary charts crammed into an old filing cabinet, jokes about his fading eyesight and supposes one day he will no longer be able to identify footballers from the gantry.

Fortunately, we are still far from that point. At 72, Tyldesley is calling the game as accurately as ever. His eyes are perfectly good when bespectacled, his mind nimble enough to keep up with play and his soothingly familiar voice strong and authoritative with a gentle tendency towards self-deprecation.

This much was evident as Manchester United roared back to beat Roma in the Champions League and a clip of his spine-tingling commentary from the live CBS broadcast circulated on social media and found an appreciative audience in Europe.

'I don't know if there's an element of nostalgia in hearing my voice again,' says Tyldesley. 'If I'm honest, I've dodged the worst of the public's ire with everything including commentators because I haven't been around for the last few years.

'Absence has made a few hearts grow a little fonder towards me and maybe if I'd been on Sky every week for the last six years, I'd be no less unpopular than anybody else out there. So, I can't pretend it's not nice to get some engagement with an audience I used to commentate to on a regular basis, but I'm very happy where I am.'

Tyldesley has been the lead commentator for the CBS coverage of the Champions League since 2020, converting transfer fees into US dollars and keeping his measurements imperial for a North American audience but otherwise approaching the job as he always did.

Clive Tyldesley is calling the game as accurately as ever at 72 and is 'very happy' in his role as the lead commentator of CBS coverage of the Champions League

Tyldesley's commentary of Man United's comeback against Roma circulated on social media and received an appreciative audience in Europe

The 72-year-old wonders whether there was an element of nostalgia to the reaction, with Tyldesley's work for CBS meaning his commentary cannot be shown in Europe

Clips of the studio panel featuring Thierry Henry, Micah Richards, Jamie Carragher and presenter Kate Scott are popular on social media but live action featuring Tyldesley's commentary is governed by broadcasting rights deals and cannot be shown in Europe.

The one from Old Trafford of Matheus Cunha's winning goal in the 86th minute slipped through the net on X and reminded everyone his passion for football is undimmed, and his voice can still stand hairs on attention.

'I don't think I've seen a better game than the first leg of the Paris Saint-Germain v Bayern Munich Champions League semi-final,' says Tyldesley on the rare quality of Europe's elite competition. 'I listened to people with hundreds more England caps than me saying it was bad defending, but I watched the whole game back the next day and it wasn't.

'I'm sorry but it was wonderful attacking and a show of intent by two coaches who trusted defenders to defend one-on-one and attackers to score more than the opposition. Rob Green was my co-commentator and at the end we just put our microphones down and looked at each other and said, "Wow."

'I've not forgotten muddy pitches and assassin centre backs. You only need to look on YouTube to see football was different, but you can't pretend it was better. I see terrible games today just as I did then, but particularly in the Champions League, I regularly stumble upon football that gets me off my seat.'

His exit from ITV, first displaced by Sam Matterface as lead commentator in 2020 and then released entirely after Euro 2024 clearly smarted but Tyldesley is comfortable as the veteran in the fast-changing media landscape.

'Most of the principles I picked up from watching John Motson, Barry Davies and Brian Moore in their pomp are applicable to commentary in 2026,' he says. 'There's no need to reinvent that particular wheel.

'You can offer alternatives such as fan zones and screaming watchalongs for people to view it in a different way. I make it my business to look at J_Tekkz or LDN Movements or whatever is pulling in millions on YouTube.

Tyldesley believes he has not seen a better game than the first leg of PSG's Champions League semi-final with Bayern Munich last year

The veteran commentator believes most of the principles he learned starting out still apply, but admits to having watched popular new voices to see if anything could apply to his commentary

Tyldesley also works as a guest lecturer and commentates for blockbuster computer games, as well as selling framed prints of his commentary charts

'I sample a bit of Mark Goldbridge to see why he's prominent but I'm hearing nothing in those guys applicable to the way I call a football match so I carry on with the same focus I've always had on what constitutes good commentary.'

The central principle being that the game is bigger than the individuals in it, he points out, with viewers tuning in for the football not the commentator.

'The biggest challenge for a television commentator is to find the right words at the big moments, to go beyond "amazing," "brilliant", "incredible" and try to add some editorial context,' says Tyldesley.

'Every goal is unique. The words following a goal that is going to be remembered for years should be unique and specific to that goal, but that's difficult to do. It's unscripted performance and difficult to master and capture.

'I am concentrating hardest for the 10-15 seconds after a big goal because I'm searching for words which will become a small part of people's memories. That's very different to consciously trying to provide 45-second soundbites to amplify one's own personality and standing on social media.

'There's a danger of media leaning that way as it develops such an emphasis on the bitesize.'

Among other things, Tyldesley is a guest lecturer for media students at the University of Salford, still doing commentaries for blockbuster computer games and selling framed prints of his commentary charts, something that started as 'a silly idea in lockdown'.

His wife Susan bought a dozen frames to see how it went. Originally, he offered three Champions League finals won by English clubs in 1999, 2005 and 2012. He sent one each to Gary Neville who played for Manchester United in 1999 and Jamie Carragher who played for Liverpool in 2005. They both posted images online and demand skyrocketed.

'Two good friends,' smiles Tyldesley. 'I probably got about half a million pounds of free advertising out of them.' Sales have soared beyond 50,000. There's a Celtic chart on the gym in Rod Stewart's house. Ant and Dec have bought signed Newcastle charts.

His own venture into podcasting was short-lived and he politely declines between five and ten invitations each week to appear on others.

'I've tried to step back from that kind of thing,' says Tyldesley. 'So much content I hear on football is empty, verbose and repetitive. Really, there are only so many things you can say about Alexander Isak having his shirt pulled in mid-air and Gary Neville probably said most of them in the 30 seconds following the incident.

Tyldesley has no plans to retire and Paramount, the owners of his employers CBS - and soon to be the owners of TNT Sports - will have the UK rights for the Champions League

Sales of his framed commentary charts, something that started during lockdown, have soared beyond 50,000

'There are so many brutally judgmental loud voices in and around football attracting attention that I want to be as far away from as possible, so that's what I do. Unless I sense an opportunity to talk about communication and broadcasting rather than whether club A, B or C should replace their manager. That's not for me Clive.'

So, there's a little less Tyldesley out there than there was. He was content to stay at home and watch the World Cup from his sofa this summer for the first time since 1990.

But there are no plans to retire. And who knows what might change next season when Paramount, the owners of CBS – and soon to be the owners of current rights holders TNT Sports – have the UK rights for the Champions League.

There might be a familiar voice beamed into our living rooms once again.

When I saw the Dear England play, I was the only person in the theatre who didn't enjoy it, and that was because I hated the portrayal of Harry Kane.

He was written as an uneducated numbskull. Written to laugh at and the theatre laughed at him. He was stupid and gullible, another thick footballer.

And anyone who has spent time with footballers will know they might lack for an Eton College education but are streetwise and invariably smart with a razor sharp sense of humour.

Kane is a leader of those men. There's not a single thing about the person Kane has made himself to laugh or sneer at and I wanted to stand up in the theatre that afternoon and shout at everyone.

Oddly, I was introduced to the playwright James Graham at a function a few weeks later and he kind of pushed me for my opinion of Dear England.

I tried to be diplomatic, but I felt so strongly I ended up scolding him for writing a character called Harry Kane who was nothing like Harry Kane.

So, that was the end of a beautiful friendship before it began. And I'm so thrilled now there's a better appreciation of the person Harry is.

#1300. Forget Left-Back: Man Utd Targeting Lankshear As First Pochettino Signing

Manchester United are monitoring the progress of Middlesbrough striker Will Lankshear ahead of a potential January move as they look to strengthen Mauricio Pochettino's squad this winter, according to TEAMtalk.

Lankshear has enjoyed an electric start to the new season at Boro after completing his switch to Riverside from Tottenham Hotspur over the summer. Netting 15 goals in his first 16 matches across all competitions, the 21-year-old is now attracting interest from a host of Premier League clubs, including United, Arsenal, Brighton, Everton, Newcastle, Leeds and Sunderland.

The Red Devils, who have just appointed Pochettino as Michael Carrick's successor, are in need of a centre-forward, with Benjamin Sesko's injury issues meaning they've been light on options for much of this campaign.

Lankshear is on their shortlist, although competition from several other clubs and Middlesbrough's likely reluctance to sell mid-season will complicate a potential deal.

After scoring 12 goals on loan at Oxford United last season, Tottenham opted to cash in on Lankshear over the summer, garnering upwards of £20 million for the young England striker.

Just a few months later, a return to the Premier League could be on the cards for the former Spurs man. An extraordinarily prolific start to the new campaign has seen Lankshear become the most-wanted talent in the Championship right now, with clubs queuing up to sign the number nine in January.

According to TEAMtalk, Tottenham have a matching-right option included in the deal they negotiated with Middlesbrough in the summer, and are therefore also in the picture regarding a future transfer.

United are yet to approach Boro about a deal, with their interest at this point said to be at preliminary stages. The Red Devils are carefully tracking Lankshear's performances, whilst they continue to assess other potential targets.

Lankshear's Statistics 2026/27 (Championship Only)

TEAMtalk suggest that Boro have no intention to sell their talismanic striker in January, as they focus on winning promotion to the English top flight. The Teesiders currently sit in the Championship's top two, level on points with Birmingham City in first and Stoke City in third. The competitive nature of this season's Championship means they may not be able to afford losing Lankshear whilst still achieving their aim of promotion.

The striker himself is understood to have shown no signs that he's ready to agitate for a move away in January.

Manchester United are expected to be busy in the January transfer window and support Mauricio Pochettino following a miserable start to the season

Pochettino will no doubt be eager to recruit a striker after arriving at Old Trafford from the USMNT. Sesko hasn't played a minute of football since mid-September, and isn't expected back until January, while Joshua Zirkzee has three Premier League goals in his last 30 appearances.

United have been forced to deploy either Bryan Mbeumo or Mateus Cunha down the middle for much of this season in Sesko's absence, an arrangement Pochettino is unlikely to want to persist with.

While left-back has been mooted as the priority position for United, it appears they could first move for a brand new centre-forward.

#1298. Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Climate change is affecting many types of crop, including these unusually small potatoes.Credit: John Thys/AFP/Getty

Policymakers at the United Nations COP31 climate conference that started this week in Antalya, Turkey, will know that the UN Environment Programme has confirmed that global warming will exceed the limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures agreed in 2015 in Paris. This meeting comes hot on the heels of the UN COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, which affirmed yet again that the world is also in the middle of a biodiversity crisis. Progress in each case, whether preventing dangerous climate change or stemming biodiversity loss, is too slow. But researchers across scientific disciplines are now arguing that advances in biotechnology could provide solutions1. Methods such as gene editing and germplasm mining — the analysis of huge libraries of plant-genome sequences to find useful traits for crop improvement — can now be used to tackle global warming and protect nature, scientists write in a climate-themed issue of Nature Biotechnology.

There was a time — not that long ago — when many considered biotechnologies a threat to the environment. But as the special issue shows, a shift is under way. Now, the field offers strategies for protecting both climate and biodiversity from the many damaging effects of industrial agriculture.

To feed a growing global population, between 2015 and 2024, the amount of cultivated land grew by roughly eight million hectares a year1. Yet, if the greenhouse-gas emissions, and thus global warming, this expansion causes is to be avoided, the world must work out how to produce enough food within its current agricultural footprint. Land clearance and land-use change contributes up to five billion tonnes of carbon annually — and is a major cause of biodiversity loss. Here, biotech solutions have some of the greatest potential, for example, by helping to increase crop yields and to protect plants from heat, drought and disease.

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

Of 77 such technologies with applications in agriculture, aquaculture and other sectors, many are ready for large-scale testing in the field, propose bioengineers Shekhar Mishra, Lauren Lui and Adam Arkin at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California in a Perspective article2. Argentina, China and the United States have given the green light to engineered drought-tolerant crops.

Rice farming produces around 9% of human-caused emissions of the greenhouse gas methane. Now, researchers have found a way to slash these emissions, write agronomist Yunkai Jin at Hunan Agricultural University in Changsha, China, and his colleagues in a Comment article3.

But technological readiness isn’t enough: governments, regulators and the public need to be ready, too4. Readers might have a sense of déjà vu: in the 1990s, advances in biotechnology promised a revolution in food and agriculture — which subsequently stalled. The ambition was to genetically modify crops or engineer them in other ways so that they could tolerate herbicides, resist insects and fight viruses. But, at the time, many scientists, governments and corporations promoting the technology gave insufficient attention to several issues.

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

One concern was public anxiety about the idea of eating food produced using transgenic technologies — crops modified by inserting a gene from another plant species or other organism. Another issue was that risks to the environment and to human health had not been studied sufficiently. A third problem was that multinational companies dominated both the research and the development of these technologies, creating fears that the rise of agricultural biotechnology would put many small family farms out of business.

Environmental groups found common cause with consumer organizations. Together, they urged governments to enact strict regulations. In the European Union, for example, risks to human health and the environment needed to be assessed before technologies producing genetically modified organisms could be commercialized. Although this was necessary, it slowed down advances in low- and middle-income countries, because any nation intending to export produce to the EU would have to prove that it was not genetically modified.

Since then, at least two things have changed, increasing optimism about the use of biotechnology to help the planet. The discovery of gene editing — in which an organism’s genes are modified precisely to produce specific traits — has proved transformational for agriculture. The method is being developed cautiously and is regulated in a more nuanced way than were conventional technologies that produce genetically modified crops. In June, the EU amended its regulations on genetic modification and now permits the cultivation of some gene-edited crops.

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

A second development is that catastrophic events such as heatwaves and floods have meant that climate change and the planet’s protection have become mainstream concerns across science and society, not just for environmental research. In a way, we all need to be environmentalists now, and this provides a rationale for governments to reconsider adopting biotech solutions with appropriate safeguards in place.

Advances in biotechnology that limit land use should be deployed to slow down the rise in global temperatures and biodiversity loss. This will require a partnership between the private sector, scientists, conservationists and farmers. High-yielding crops produced using industrial agriculture have helped to feed the world but have also had a devastating effect on biodiversity. Organic agriculture is more sustainable but requires extra land, because its yields tend to be lower than those from industrial methods. Providing they are implemented wisely, safely and ethically, biotechnologies could contribute to innovative farming methods that offer the best of both worlds.

#1297. Super Mario! Dons hand rebuild job to Swiss success story Frick

Published: 14:14 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 14:45 EST, 15 November 2026

Aberdeen have appointed former Liechtenstein international Mario Frick as their new head coach.

The 52-year-old will take charge at Pittodrie, subject to the completion of UK visa formalities, following a successful spell with Swiss side FC Luzern.

Frick arrives in the north-east after five years in charge of Luzern, where he transformed the club’s fortunes after taking over in December 2021 with the team rooted to the bottom of the Swiss Super League. He guided them away from relegation trouble before leading them to a fourth-place finish and qualification for European football.

Announcing the appointment, Aberdeen chief executive Adrian Bevington said the club had undertaken an extensive recruitment process before selecting Frick as the man to lead the Dons forward.

Bevington said: 'We are delighted to welcome Mario Frick and his assistant coach Roman Matter to Aberdeen Football Club.

'Mario has significant experience as a head coach and has delivered impressive results with both Vaduz and Luzern. He has a proven track record of building competitive teams and developing young players.

'Throughout our discussions, he demonstrated a clear vision, strong leadership qualities and a deep understanding of what is required to build a successful team.'

Sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel also welcomed the appointment and believes Frick has the qualities to make a major impact at Pittodrie.

Pfannenstiel said: 'Mario is a strong personality with clear ideas about how he wants his teams to play. He brings energy, ambition and a winning mentality, and knows how to build a strong team environment.

Aberdeen have appointed Mario Frick as their new manager

'We were looking for the right person to lead the next chapter of Aberdeen FC, and I’m convinced Mario has the qualities, character and vision to make a real impact.'

Before his spell with Luzern, Frick managed FC Balzers and FC Vaduz, winning promotion to the Swiss Super League with the latter. Across almost 290 senior matches as a head coach, he built a reputation for developing young talent, handing top-flight debuts to more than 30 academy players.

As a player, Frick represented clubs including FC Basel, FC Zürich, St Gallen, Grasshopper, Siena and Ternana. A striker who could also operate in defence, he won 125 caps for Liechtenstein between 1993 and 2016 and remains his country’s record goalscorer with 16 international goals.

Frick said: 'I’m excited to be joining Aberdeen FC. It’s a club with a proud history, passionate supporters and big ambitions.

'Together with the staff, my aim is to create an environment where the players can thrive, develop and perform at their very best, while working towards our goals as a team.'

Frick and assistant coach Matter are expected to arrive in Aberdeen at the start of the week and will begin preparations for next weekend’s Premiership clash with Kilmarnock.
